A red herring is something — a clue, a piece of information, an argument, or a detail — that seems important or relevant but is actually a distraction. It pulls your attention away from the real issue, the real question, or the real answer.

The crucial word here is seems. A red herring doesn't look like a distraction on the surface. It appears connected to what matters. That's exactly what makes it so effective and so tricky. If it were obviously irrelevant, nobody would fall for it.

Think of it like a false path in a maze. Someone is trying to find the truth, solve a problem, or follow an argument. A red herring pulls them down a path that leads nowhere. Once they follow it, they're wasting time and energy on something that has nothing to do with the real answer.

In arguments and debates

This is one of the most common uses. When someone doesn't want to answer a difficult question, or when they're losing a debate, they bring up a completely unrelated point to shift attention elsewhere.

Example:

Person A: "You've been late to work three times this week."
Person B: "Well, you were sick for two days last month!"

Person B's point about being sick is a red herring. It doesn't address the lateness at all. It just changes the subject so that Person A feels defensive and forgets the original point.

Another common example, from politics:

Journalist: "Why did the government raise taxes?"
Politician: "What we should really be talking about is how the previous government mismanaged the economy."

The politician doesn't answer the question. They redirect attention to a different topic entirely.

In logic and critical thinking, this is formally known as the red herring fallacy — it's when someone introduces irrelevant information into a discussion specifically to mislead or distract.

In mysteries and detective fiction

This is probably the most famous use of the term. In mystery novels, films, and TV shows, writers deliberately plant red herrings. These are fake clues — details designed to make you believe they're important to solving the crime, when in fact they lead you to the wrong conclusion.

Example: In a murder mystery, a nervous character who was seen near the crime scene seems like the obvious suspect. You spend the whole story convinced it's them. But at the end, they're completely innocent — they were nervous because of an unrelated personal secret. The author planted them as a red herring to fool you.

Agatha Christie, one of the greatest mystery writers, was a master at this. She carefully scattered misleading clues throughout her novels so that even sharp readers would be surprised by the ending. In this sense, a red herring is a storytelling tool — used intentionally to create suspense and surprise.

In everyday life

Red herrings appear all the time in ordinary conversations, not just in debates or fiction.

Example: A parent asks their child, "Did you eat the last of the cookies?" The child replies, "I cleaned my room today!"

Cleaning the room is true, and it's a good thing — but it's a red herring. It doesn't answer the question about the cookies at all. It's just a distraction, possibly used to avoid admitting the truth.

Red herrings can work in two different ways:

  • Deliberately: Someone knowingly introduces a distraction to mislead you, avoid a topic, or manipulate the conversation. This is often done dishonestly — the person knows they're dodging the real issue.
  • Accidentally: Someone brings up something they genuinely believe is relevant, but it actually isn't. They're not trying to deceive — they're simply confused about what matters to the discussion.

In both cases, the result is the same: attention moves away from the real issue.
A critical nuance: a red herring doesn't have to be false

This is something many people overlook, and it's important for real understanding.

A red herring is not necessarily a lie. It can be a completely true statement — it just isn't relevant to the point being discussed.

Example:

Question: "Should we invest in renewable energy?"
Response: "Well, scientists have been wrong about things before."

The response is factually true — scientists have been wrong sometimes. But that truth has nothing to do with whether we should invest in renewable energy today. It's a true statement being used as a red herring.

This is what separates a red herring from a plain lie: a lie is false; a red herring may be true but is simply irrelevant.
How to spot a red herring

Whenever you're in a conversation, reading a mystery, watching an interview, or following a debate, train yourself to ask one simple question:

"Does this point actually address the original question or issue?"

If the answer is no — if the new information doesn't connect to what was originally being discussed — you've likely encountered a red herring.

A few signs to watch for:

  • The topic suddenly shifts to something else mid-conversation.
  • Someone responds to a direct question by raising a completely different question.
  • You feel like the original problem is being ignored, even though the person is speaking confidently about something.
  • You find yourself forgetting what you originally asked.

Once you catch yourself thinking "wait, how did we get here?" — that's often a red herring doing its job.
How it's used as a phrase

You'll encounter "red herring" in sentences like these:

  • "The broken window was just a red herring — the thief had actually entered through the back door."
  • "Don't fall for that argument, it's a classic red herring."
  • "The author planted several red herrings to keep readers guessing until the final chapter."
  • "Bringing up last year's budget is a red herring — it has nothing to do with today's proposal."

A red herring is anything — a clue, a statement, an argument, a detail, a character — that appears significant or relevant but actually misleads you or distracts you from the truth or the real issue.

It can be used:

  • Deliberately — to deceive, manipulate, or avoid a topic
  • Accidentally — when someone doesn't realise something is off-topic
  • Artistically — by writers and filmmakers to create suspense and surprise

It doesn't have to be false — it just has to be irrelevant. And the moment you recognise it for what it is and return your focus to the actual question, the red herring loses all its power.
